!!! success "Check"
    After connecting real hardware, the state and identity belong to your driver. If they do not appear, check
    the transport, the selected port, the supply and the TX/RX wiring before trying to move.

## Try it without hardware

Open [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), choose **Mock CAN (demo)**, and press **Connect**. The motor and gripper panels run in the browser without a port picker. Motor calibration (`#Cal`) still requires a real UART connection; the CAN demo does not perform it.

## What next

[Motor parameters and calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/) is the first thing to do with a connected driver;
[Working in Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/motor-gui/) covers everyday use: moving the motor, the plots, recordings,
several motors on a bus.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/terminal/ -->

# The serial terminal

Motor GUI is the usual way to work with the driver; a plain serial terminal is the alternative, and it is what
the console inside Motor GUI is. Everything in this manual that is done in the GUI is also one `#` command, and
the terminal shows the driver's answers exactly as it prints them, which is useful when something does not work.

The driver talks on its UART connector at 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V. Any terminal that sends a line ending in
CR+LF works.

![The UART connector. TX of the driver goes to RX of the adapter and RX to TX.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/STEPFOC_UART.webp){ width="900" }

## Connecting

1. Plug the [USB-to-serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) into the UART
   connector with the [UART cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/uart-cable). With another adapter: 3.3 V
   only, and cross TX and RX: the driver's TX to the adapter's RX, the driver's RX to the adapter's TX.
2. Connect the motor supply. The adapter's 3.3 V powers the driver's logic, so the driver answers over UART with
   only the adapter plugged in, but it reports a Vbus error and refuses calibration and every motion command
   until the 12 to 29 V supply is on.
3. Find the adapter's port:

=== "Windows"
    The adapter is `COM` and a number. Device Manager lists it under **Ports (COM & LPT)**: the entry that
    disappears when you unplug the adapter is yours. An adapter that shows a warning sign there instead needs the
    driver of its USB chip (on most 3.3 V adapters a CP210x or a CH340) from the chip maker.

=== "Linux"
    The serial adapter is `/dev/ttyUSB0` on most adapters, the CANvas adapter `/dev/ttyACM0`;
    `ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM*` lists them. To open them without root, join the `dialout` group once, then
    log out and in again:

    ```
    sudo usermod -aG dialout $USER
    ```

=== "macOS"
    The serial adapter is `/dev/cu.usbserial-` and a few characters on most adapters, the CANvas adapter
    `/dev/cu.usbmodem` and a number; `ls /dev/cu.*` lists them. Use the `cu.` name, not the `tty.` one, in a
    terminal or a script.

!!! danger
    5 V on the UART pins destroys the board.

## A terminal

=== "PuTTY"
    PuTTY needs to send CR+LF when you press Enter, which the stock build cannot. Use the
    [modified PuTTY](https://www.grzegorz.net/pliki/putty-crlf.zip): under *Terminal → Keyboard* select the CR LF
    option, then open the serial port at 256000.

    | Keyboard setting | Session |
    |---|---|
    | ![PuTTY keyboard tab](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/PUTTY2.PNG){ width="420" } | ![PuTTY session](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/PUTTY1.PNG){ width="420" } |

=== "VS Code (PlatformIO)"
    With the [firmware project](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/bootloader-version/STEPFOC%20firmware)
    open in VS Code with the PlatformIO extension, the serial monitor (the plug icon in the status bar) uses the
    speed and the `send_on_enter` filter from `platformio.ini`, so a line goes out with CR+LF when you press
    Enter.

    | platformio.ini | The monitor |
    |---|---|
    | ![platformio.ini](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/vscode1.PNG){ width="420" } | ![The serial monitor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/vscode2.PNG){ width="420" } |

=== "Arduino IDE"
    Select the adapter's port under *Tools*, any board (the monitor does not care), open the serial monitor, set
    256000 baud and *Both NL & CR* as the line ending.

    ![The Arduino serial monitor at 256000 baud, with Both NL & CR as the line ending](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/Arduino3.PNG){ width="420" }

## The first commands

```
#Info
```

prints the driver's identity and state: the hardware and firmware version, the CAN ID, the calibration state and
the motor parameters. `#Help` (firmware 106 and newer) prints a short command reference, `#Error` the active
errors, `#Param` the gains and limits.

!!! success "Check"
    `#Info` answers with the driver's identity, the hardware and firmware version first. If nothing comes back:
    the baud rate, the CR+LF line ending, TX and RX, see
    [The driver does not answer](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/#the-driver-does-not-answer).

Every command starts with `#`, and a Set/Get command takes one number after a space: `#P 16384` moves to position
16384; `#P` alone prints the position. Names are case-sensitive. The whole set is in the
[UART commands](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/uart/) reference, and [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/uart/) explains the
protocol.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/ -->

# Motor parameters and calibration

Calibration teaches the driver its motor: it checks the magnet and the supply, takes the motor's resistance,
inductance and pole pairs from you, computes the current loop gains, spins the motor in open loop to learn the
direction of the wiring, finds the angle offset between the encoder and the motor's electrical zero, and measures
the motor constants Kt, KV and the flux linkage. From firmware 109 two more runs follow by themselves, the
[encoder table and the anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/anti-cogging/), and then the driver saves everything. It runs once per
motor; the result is kept by saving.

!!! danger "The motor turns"
    Calibration spins the motor in both directions, fast at times. Fix the motor to the bench and take everything
    off the shaft.

!!! tip "Supply voltage"
    Calibrate at 24 V. From firmware 109 KV and Kt no longer depend on the supply or on `#Vlim`: the spins that
    measure them run at their own 6 V limit, and yours is put back afterwards.

## 1. Restore the defaults

The EEPROM of a new driver, or of one that ran another motor, can hold values that do not fit, such as another
motor's parameters. Calibration starts from what is there, so start from the factory values. (A damaged
configuration should not show up with firmware 106 and newer, which checks the stored blocks at power-up and
replaces a damaged one with the defaults; if `#Info` still shows `-1` somewhere, restoring the defaults fixes it.)

=== "Motor GUI"
    *Default* in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Default
    ```

This also resets the serial number, hardware version and batch date stored in the EEPROM, and clears an
encoder table and an anti-cogging set from another motor; note the hardware version and batch date `#Info`
prints if you need them. From firmware 109 the CAN node ID is kept. [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/saving/) says
what else it does.

## 2. Enter the motor parameters

STEPFOC does not measure the resistance and inductance of a stepper (the Spectral Micro does for a BLDC); you
enter them from the motor's datasheet, as the values of **one coil**, and the pole pairs. Calibration fails on a
value left at 0, and accepts only 50, 75, 100 or 125 pole pairs.

=== "Motor GUI"
    In the motor settings enter *Pole pairs* (50 for a 1.8° motor, 75 for 1.2°, 100 for 0.9°, 125 for 0.72°),
    *Resistance* in ohms and *Inductance* in henries, and apply them.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #PP 50          1.8° stepper: 50; 1.2°: 75; 0.9°: 100; 0.72°: 125
    #R 1.1          phase resistance in ohms
    #L 0.0026       phase inductance in henries (2.6 mH)
    ```

=== "CAN"
    Parameters 78 (pole pairs), 76 (resistance in mΩ) and 77 (inductance in µH) hold the same values, for a
    host that sets a drive up over the bus: Send_Parameter(78, 50), Send_Parameter(76, 1100),
    Send_Parameter(77, 2600). The calibration itself runs over the serial port.

![The three values on a typical datasheet, here for the 17HS16-2004S1: 1.8°, 1.1 Ω, 2.6 mH.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/Motor_specs.webp){ width="900" }

Calibration computes the current loop gains from R, L and the current loop bandwidth, 160 Hz by default:
Kp = ω·L and Ki = ω·R, with ω = 2π × the bandwidth. The firmware keeps Ki per control loop, so `Ki_iq` in the
log is about ω·R × 160 µs. Leave the bandwidth for now;
[Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/) comes back to it. (Firmware 108 and older divided both gains by 7,
which gave a loop of about 70 Hz.)

## 3. Run it

=== "Motor GUI"
    Start the calibration. The driver enters *Calibration mode* and the GUI shows its log step by step; when it
    finishes, the phase order and direction, Kt, KV and the flux linkage it found appear in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Cal
    ```

The LED flashes fast while the routine runs, and the driver prints each step as it goes:

```
----------------
Calibration mode
----------------
Pole pair test: Passed
Magnet test: Passed
Vbus test: Passed
Resistance = 1.100000Ohm
Inductance = 0.002600H
Kp_iq = ...
Ki_iq = ...
Open loop direction: good
Calibrating angle offset... stage 1/13, sweep point 0
...
Angle offset is: ...
Alignment check: ... ticks/s, flipped ..., offsets ... / ...
Phase order is good!
KV is: ...
Kt is: ...
KV runs: ... ... ... ... (same direction within ... %)
Flux linkage is: ...
----------------
Calibration success!
Next, by itself: the encoder table, then anti-cogging (about a minute; keep the shaft free). Everything is saved when they finish (#Encal state, #Cogcal state)
Going to idle!
----------------
```

`#Calonly` runs the same calibration and nothing after it; it ends with `Save config with #Save` instead.

What the steps are:

| Step | What happens | Fails with |
|---|---|---|
| Pole pair test | the entered pole pairs are one of 50, 75, 100, 125 | `Pole pair test: Failed` and the list of values |
| Magnet test | the encoder sees enough field: a magnet is there and close enough. The test says nothing about centring, the gap or the glue | `Magnet test: Failed`: magnet missing, too far, or axially magnetised |
| Vbus test | the supply is within limits | `Vbus test: Failed` |
| Resistance, inductance | the entered values are not 0; they are printed back and Kp_iq, Ki_iq computed from them and the bandwidth | `Resistance test: Failed` / `Inductance test: Failed`, with `Please enter your stepper resistance by using #R command` |
| Open loop | the motor is stepped open loop at a fixed 5000 mV. The direction the encoder saw is remembered, so a reversed coil is compensated from here on | nothing in this firmware: the step always reports `good`, and a motor that did not turn fails the next step |
| Angle offset | a short spin checks that the motor turns (two tries, 90 electrical degrees apart); then the field locks the rotor and a sweep finds the offset at which both directions turn alike. It prints `Calibrating angle offset...` with its progress every half second | `Phase order is wrong!` / `Switch motor phases and try again!`: the motor did not turn on either try. A line `Spin-confirm delta: … ticks (need > 8192), Vbus: … mV` says how far it turned and at what voltage. When the lock or the check after it fails instead, `Angle alignment gave up:` names the reason (`it timed out`, `the rotor did not turn under current` or `the rotor turned the wrong way, also after flipping`), followed by `Check speed … ticks/s (need > 1000), flipped …, offsets … rad` and `Try again; if it repeats, check the motor, its wiring and that the shaft is free` |
| Kt, KV, flux linkage | four spins from standstill at 500 mA, about a second each and alternately forward and back, at a 6 V limit; KV is the mean speed per volt, Kt follows as 8.27 ÷ KV and the flux linkage from Kt. `KV runs:` in the log shows all four and how far they agree | nothing: `KV runs differ by more than 5 %: calibrate again, and check that the shaft is free` is a warning, and the calibration still succeeds |

A whole run takes up to about a minute, most of it in the angle-offset search. When a step fails, the log ends
with `Calibration failed!`, the driver goes to idle, the motor counts as not calibrated and the LED stays on
steadily. Nothing is saved; fix the cause and run `#Cal` again.

!!! note "The 'Switch motor phases' message"
    It is left over from firmware 103, which needed the coils wired a particular way. Since firmware 105 the
    wiring is detected and compensated, so `Phase order is wrong!` / `Switch motor phases and try again!` means the
    motor did not turn or did not respond: a coil not connected or shorted, a supply too weak, or a magnet that
    slips. Swapping wires does not fix it. (`Open loop: Failed` with the same advice cannot appear in this
    release.)

!!! note "The measured values are estimates"
    KV, Kt and the flux linkage come from one short spin and differ a little from one run to the next, more on
    motors with uneven windings. For the loops this does not matter; for a torque estimate in newton-metres,
    measure Kt yourself.

## What follows the calibration

Half a second after `Calibration success!` of a `#Cal` the driver starts two runs on its own: the encoder table
(about 20 s), then the anti-cogging identification with the current-sense zero trim (about 25 to 70 s). When they
succeed, everything is saved.

The motor turns slowly, one turn forward and one back for each run, so keep the shaft free for about a minute
more; `#Info` shows `running: …` under `In force:` while they go. A command from a host (a motion command,
`#Idle`) stops them; then nothing is saved, and the calibration is kept only if you `#Save` it.
[Encoder table and anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/anti-cogging/) explains both and how to check them. `#Cal` always runs them;
`#Calonly` never does.

!!! warning "Set the current limit before you calibrate"
    The encoder table turns the field with a current of 80 % of the current limit, for about 20 s. Calibration uses
    its own 1600 mA for its steps and puts the limit that was in force back when it ends, before the encoder table
    runs; after `#Default` that is 1700 mA, about 1.4 A in the coils, more than a small motor is rated for. So set
    `#Ilim` for the motor before `#Cal` (a Motor GUI preset does; known issue KI-19).

!!! note "Not yet tested on the bench"
    The runs after a calibration and `#Calonly` were tested on the bench on 2026-11-10 (`#Calonly` 25 times on a
    20 mm motor, `#Cal` with both runs on a 40 mm and a 60 mm motor). Parameters 76 to 79 and `#Par` came last in
    firmware 109 and had not been tested on the bench when this page was written.

## 4. Save

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Save**. The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you do.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Save
    ```

After `#Cal` the driver saves by itself when the runs succeed; save anyway once they are done, or after
`#Calonly`. Without a save the calibration is gone at the next power cycle.
The driver goes to idle and the LED shows normal operation; the state shows *Calibrated* and the constants.

!!! warning "The current limit"
    Calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its steps. From firmware 109 it puts the limit that was in force back when
    it ends, so a save stores your limit; firmware 108 and older left 1600 mA in force (known issue KI-2). If the
    limit is still the 1700 mA of `#Default`, set it for your motor with `#Ilim` and save again
    ([Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/)).

!!! success "Check"
    After a power cycle `#Info` prints `Calibrated` and the constants calibration found, and Motor GUI shows
    *Calibrated*. `Not calibrated` means the save did not happen: calibrate and save again.

## When to calibrate again

- After changing the motor, the magnet or the wiring.
- After restoring the defaults.
- After a firmware update that clears the calibration (a release note says so when it does).

A calibration that reports success but a motor that runs badly afterwards usually means the magnet moved on the
shaft between calibration and use: fix the magnet and calibrate again.

## Troubleshooting

| Message | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Magnet test: Failed` | no magnet, magnet too far (more than about 1.5 mm), or an axially magnetised magnet |
| `Vbus test: Failed` | supply off, too low, or the cable the wrong way round (if the driver survived it) |
| `Resistance test: Failed`, `Inductance test: Failed` | the resistance or the inductance still 0 |
| `Phase order is wrong!` | see the note above: the motor did not turn on the spin check; check the four wires and their solder joints, the supply and its current limit, and the magnet |
| `Angle alignment gave up:` after `Phase order is wrong!` | the lock or the check after it failed, and the line names the reason; run `#Cal` again, and if it repeats check the motor, its wiring and that the shaft is free |
| `Cal: not started, the E-stop is latched (#Clear first)`, or `Stopped by an E-stop: #Clear, then calibrate again.` after `Calibration failed!` | an E-stop is latched or ended the calibration: `#Clear`, then `#Cal`; the alignment starts again from its first stage |
| the routine stops in a step and prints nothing more | reset the driver (`#Reset`) and try again; the angle-offset search prints a progress line every half second, so wait for a minute before you decide |
| success, but the LED stays on and no error is reported | should not happen with firmware 106 and newer, which replaces a damaged configuration block with the defaults at power-up. If `#Info` shows `-1` somewhere, restore the defaults, enter the parameters and calibrate again |

`#Calangle` runs an angle-offset search on its own, with an older routine than the one `#Cal` uses: it gives up
after about two minutes and keeps the offset it reached. From firmware 109, when parameter 56 is not 0, the
anti-cogging is identified again afterwards and everything is saved, because the anti-cogging depends on the
offset. After a timeout nothing follows and nothing is saved. From firmware 109 `#Calangle` is refused while the
driver is in error: it prints `Calangle: not started, the drive is in error (#Error, #Clear)`. After a change of
motor, magnet or wiring, run the whole `#Cal` instead.

Calibration runs over the serial connection only: a terminal, or Motor GUI over the serial adapter, not over CAN.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/anti-cogging/ -->

# Encoder table and anti-cogging

Firmware 109 measures two corrections on the drive itself, with nothing but the motor on the bench: the
**encoder table**, which corrects the small error of the encoder's angle reading, and the **anti-cogging**, a
current that cancels the motor's own torque ripple. After a calibration both run by themselves
([What follows the calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/#what-follows-the-calibration)); this page explains what they are,
how to run them again, and how to check them.

!!! danger "The motor turns"
    Each run turns the motor one revolution forward and one back, slowly. Keep the shaft free: nothing on it and
    nothing it could drive. A mechanism that cannot turn a whole revolution, a gripper's racks for example, has to
    come off first.

## The encoder table

The magnetic encoder reads the shaft angle with a small error that changes slowly around the turn: the magnet is
never exactly on the axis, and the chip itself is not perfectly linear. On the bench NEMA 17 it was 0.65° peak to
peak. The commutation multiplies it by the pole pairs, so on a 50-pole-pair stepper the field is up to 32
electrical degrees off at places, which costs torque and makes the current uneven around the turn.

To measure it, the driver turns the field open loop, one shaft revolution forward and one back at 2048 ticks/s
(about 20 s), with a current of 80 % of the current limit holding the rotor to the field. At each 1/128 of a turn
it records how far the encoder's angle is from the field's. Forward and backward are averaged, so friction, which
pulls the rotor behind the field in each direction, cancels; the stepper's own pull towards its detents is left
out by keeping only the harmonics 1 to 16 per turn. The result is a table of 128 corrections. From then on the
encoder reading is corrected with it, and the electrical offset is moved by the table's mean error, so the
commutation stays right.

A table over 4° peak to peak, or one that would move the offset by more than 60 electrical degrees, is rejected
as implausible: the magnet is loose or far off its place.

## Anti-cogging

A stepper pulls towards its detent positions, four times per electrical turn, and errors in the current
measurement add a ripple once and twice per electrical turn. At low speed both show as a ripple in the speed and
the position. Anti-cogging adds a current to the current setpoint that cancels it: a function of the electrical
angle, added in velocity and position modes.

To find it, the driver runs in velocity mode at 1500 ticks/s (parameter 44), records the current the velocity
loop asks for in 256 bins over the electrical angle for one motor revolution forward and one back, and averages
the two directions, each without its mean, so friction drops out. From that it keeps two forms of the same
correction:

- **harmonics** (parameter 37 = 1): the 8 largest of the harmonics 1 to 32 of the electrical angle, each
  a·cos(h·θ) + b·sin(h·θ) in mA;
- **table** (parameter 37 = 2): 256 values in mA over one electrical turn, interpolated between them.

The identification switches the harmonics on. On the bench both forms were equally good. Parameter 38 scales the
correction from 0 to 200 % for experiments; 100 % is as identified.

The angle here comes from the encoder alone, without the calibration's offset. The part of the correction that
comes from the current measurement is tied to the motor's electrical angle, though, which the offset defines:
that is why `#Calangle` identifies the anti-cogging again.

The identification records the current the loops ask for, so it depends a little on the gains. After a large
change of the current or velocity gains, identify it again.

### The current-sense zero trim

The once-per-electrical-turn part of the anti-cogging is mostly an error of the current-sense zero (on the bench
1.6 mA of ripple per ADC count of zero error). The identification **with the trim** reads both zero errors from it,
corrects the zeros, and identifies again on the corrected zeros.
If the 1st harmonic did not drop by at least 30 % and is still above 2.0 mA,
the zeros go back and the anti-cogging is identified once more without the trim; the state then reads 11, done
without the trim. A 1st harmonic under 1.5 mA is left alone, and one run moves a zero by at most 30 counts. The
trims (parameters 59 and 60, up to ±60 counts) are saved with the encoder table and added to the zero the driver
measures at every start-up. On the bench drive the trim took the 1st harmonic from 8.8 to 0.2 mA in one run.

## Running them

The driver must be calibrated and without an error. Both runs keep the CAN watchdog fed while they go, end by
holding the position the shaft reached, and stop at once when a host sends a command (a motion command, Idle) or
an error comes up; nothing is saved then. While a run turns the motor a capture is not armed, and during the
anti-cogging run parameters 34 and 35 refuse a write: the runs use the capture's memory and the histogram.

| What | UART | CAN: Send_Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| the encoder table, used at once | `#Encal` | 52 = 1 |
| the encoder table, used and saved | `#Encal save` | 52 = 2 |
| the encoder table, then the anti-cogging with the trim, then save all | `#Encal all` | 52 = 3, or 43 = 3 |
| the anti-cogging, switched on | `#Cogcal` | 43 = 1 |
| the anti-cogging, switched on and saved | `#Cogcal save` | 43 = 2 |
| the anti-cogging with the trim | `#Cogcal trim` | 43 = 4 |
| the anti-cogging with the trim, saved | `#Par 43,5` | 43 = 5 |
| stop a run | `#Encal stop`, `#Cogcal stop` | 52 = 0, 43 = 0 |

A save from a run is the whole configuration, as `#Save` writes it. After a change of the motor, the magnet or
its position, run the encoder table and the anti-cogging again, in that order, or calibrate again.

Two guards keep a correction from running on the wrong data: parameter 37 refuses 1 or 2 while no set is stored
for that form, and an encoder table measured on its own (52 = 1 or 2) switches an anti-cogging set from before
off, because that set was found on the uncorrected encoder; the anti-cogging state then reads 10 until it is
identified again.

## Checking them

`#Info` ends with what is in force:

```
In force:
  encoder table: on, error 0.61 deg p-p
  anti-cogging: on (harmonics), saved
  current-sense zero trim: -1 / 5 counts
  delay compensation: 166 us
  speed estimate: direct PLL, 60 Hz
  fast reading / fast PWM: on / on
  input filter: off; integral deadband: off
  after #Calangle (parameter 56): anti-cogging, then save
```

(here with the values the bench drive measured). While a run goes, a line `running: encoder table` or
`running: anti-cogging identification` follows. `#Encal state` and `#Cogcal state` print one run's state without
starting it; after a finished identification (state 3, or 11 without the trim) it also lists the harmonics.

Over CAN the same is in the parameters (the [parameter table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/parameters/#every-parameter)):

| Parameter | What it tells | On the bench NEMA 17 |
|---|---|---|
| 52 | the encoder table's state: 3 done, 4 aborted, 5 error or not calibrated, 6 the rotor did not follow, 7 rejected | 3 |
| 54, 55 | the table's error peak to peak and its once-per-turn part, 0.01° of the shaft | 61-65 (0.61-0.65°); two runs within 0.021° |
| 57 | how far the last table moved the electrical offset, 0.1° electrical | −25, then −1 on a second run |
| 43 | the anti-cogging state: 3 done, 11 done without the trim, 6 the shaft did not turn | 3 |
| 45 | the cogging current found, 0.1 mA rms | 71 (7.1 mA) |
| 62, 63 | the 1st harmonic before and after the trim, 0.1 mA | 88, then 2 |
| 59, 60 | the zero trims, counts | −1, 5 |
| 79 | the bits of what is in force, see [What is in force](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/parameters/#what-is-in-force-parameter-79) | |

With the anti-cogging on, the bench motor's speed ripple that repeats with the angle was 1.2 to 2 times smaller
at 1500 to 6000 ticks/s, and the position ripple 1.9 to 2.5 times smaller. A free motor gains little from the
encoder table in these numbers (its current varied 2.5 to 3 times less around the turn, but a free motor needs
little current); a loaded one gains more.

Send_Buffer_Read reads the corrections themselves: kind 4 the encoder table (128 values in 1/16 count), kind 2
the harmonics, kind 3 the anti-cogging table ([Respond_Buffer_Data](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/parameters/#respond_buffer_data)).

When a run fails:

| State | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 52 = 6, 43 = 6 | the rotor did not follow: the shaft is blocked, or the current is too low to turn it | free the shaft; for the encoder table raise the current limit (it uses 80 % of it) |
| 52 = 5, 43 = 5 | the driver was in error or is not calibrated | `#Error`, clear it, calibrate |
| 52 = 4, 43 = 4 | a command came first | run it again and send nothing meanwhile |
| 52 = 7 | the table is implausible | check the magnet: glued, centred, at the right distance ([The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/04-mounting/magnet/)), then calibrate |
| 43 = 8 | the encoder table of a combined run failed | parameter 52 says why |

## Switching them off

| | UART | CAN: Send_Parameter |
|---|---|---|
| the encoder table off / on | `#Encal off`, `#Encal on` | 53 = 0, 53 = 1 |
| the anti-cogging off, harmonics, table | `#Par 37,0`, `#Par 37,1`, `#Par 37,2` | 37 = 0, 1, 2 |
| how much of the anti-cogging | `#Par 38,` and the percentage | 38 = 0 to 200 (%) |

`#Save` keeps the switches with the corrections. `#Default` clears both corrections and the trims.

!!! note "Spectral Micro"
    The Spectral Micro firmware 109 has the same encoder table and anti-cogging, but runs neither after a
    calibration until they are tested on its bench, and skips the zero trim. Its manual says more.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/ -->

# Current limit and loop tuning

Calibration leaves the driver with current loop gains computed for your motor and with velocity and position
gains that suit a bare stepper. Two things remain: the current limit, which you must set for your motor, and the
loop gains, which you tune if the defaults do not suit it. Motor GUI shows the motor's response on its plots while
you change a gain, which is what makes tuning quick.

## The current limit

Set the current limit to the rated phase current of your motor in mA (the datasheet value; the tested motors'
ratings are in [Tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/03-technical-data/tested-motors/)). It is 1700 mA after `#Default`;
calibration uses its own 1600 mA for its steps and, from firmware 109, puts your limit back when it ends. Set it
before you calibrate: the encoder table that follows a calibration runs at 80 % of it. `#Ilim` clamps the limit to
the driver's 2800 mA and takes the magnitude of a negative number. The
firmware does not trip on phase current by itself and does not monitor the driver stage. A limit above the motor's
rating overheats the motor.

!!! note "Over CAN"
    From firmware 109 Send_Limits stops the current limit at 2800 mA, as `#Ilim` does, and ignores a negative
    value. Firmware 108 and older stored it as sent (known issue KI-1). A host program must still keep it within
    the motor's rating.

=== "Motor GUI"
    In the limits set the current limit, then **Save**.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Ilim 1500
    #Save
    ```

Crunching and whining sounds at speed usually mean the current limit, or the current loop gains, are too high.

## The loops

![The position loop commands the velocity loop, which commands the current loop.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/cascadeloop.webp){ width="800" }

Tune from the inside out: the current loop first, then velocity, then position. Before you start:

- The motor must be calibrated and without active errors; the driver refuses the control modes otherwise.
- Fix the motor to the bench, nothing on the shaft. A loop that oscillates can shake a loose motor off the table.
- If the defaults oscillate, lower all gains until the motor is quiet, then raise them one at a time in small steps.

=== "Motor GUI"
    The gains are in the settings: change one, *Apply gains*, command a move with the jog controls and read the
    response on the plots. *Apply preset* loads a starting set for a kind of motor: a product preset writes its
    own current and velocity gains; the *Generic motor* presets set soft limits and velocity gains and leave the
    current gains to `#Cbw` and the calibration. Apply a preset before you calibrate, so that the calibration
    computes the current gains, and set the velocity gains after it. **Save** when you are done.

=== "Terminal"
    Each gain is a command: `#Kpiq 0.5`, `#Kpv 0.02`, …, then `#Save`. Command a move with `#Iq`, `#V` or `#P`
    and judge the response by ear and by `#Cyc 20`, which streams position, speed and current.

### The current loop

The current loop is a PI controller that turns a current request into a voltage. Its gains `Kpiq` and `Kiiq`
follow from the motor's resistance R, its inductance L and one number, the bandwidth: Kp = ω·L and Ki = ω·R, with
ω = 2π × the bandwidth. The firmware keeps Ki per control loop: `Kiiq` is about ω·R × 160 µs. For 1.1 Ω, 2.6 mH
and 160 Hz that gives `Kpiq` 2.70 and `Kiiq` 0.177. Do not enter ω·R as `#Kiiq`. The PI then cancels the coil's
own lag, and the current follows a request like a first-order filter at that bandwidth. Calibration computes
them this way at 160 Hz, the default; so does setting the bandwidth:

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Cbw 200          new gains at once from R and L; it prints them
    #Save             keeps the gains (the bandwidth itself is 160 again after a power cycle)
    ```

=== "CAN"
    Send_Parameter(49, 200), then Send_Save_config. Reading parameter 49 gives the bandwidth the gains in force
    amount to with the R and L in force.

The bandwidth can be 10 to 625 Hz (a tenth of the 6250 Hz control loop). A higher one follows a request and
rejects a disturbance faster, and is louder; on the bench, 160 Hz followed an injected ripple better than the old
gains and stayed stable. Gains set by hand with `#Kpiq` and `#Kiiq` work too; parameter 49 then tells which
bandwidth they amount to.

!!! note "Drives calibrated with older firmware"
    Firmware 108 and older divided both gains by 7, a loop of about 70 Hz. Their saved gains stay as they are
    after an update to 109: parameter 49 reads about 71 Hz until the drive is calibrated again, or `#Cbw 160` and
    `#Save` are sent. See [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/upgrading/).

Test with a current setpoint of a few hundred mA (*Jog current*, or `#Iq 300`): the motor should push with a
steady, quiet torque. Keep the current well under the limit.

### The velocity loop

The firmware's start values are `Kpv` 0.02 and `Kiv` 0.001, tuned on the bench with a bare NEMA 17 and the speed
estimate below: it vibrated at `Kpv` 0.056, and 0.02 is about half of that; `Kiv` rang at 0.004, and 0.001 halved
the speed ripple at 300 to 1500 ticks/s. `#Default` and a settings reset write the same values. A drive saved
with older firmware keeps its saved gains after an update (typically 0.007 and 0.0005): set `#Kpv 0.02` and
`#Kiv 0.001` and `#Save` (a 21.5 mm stepper overshot 95 % at these on the bench; its presets use `#Kpv 0.014`
and `#Kiv 0.00014`). To tune for your motor and load:

1. Raise `Kpv` until the motor vibrates at a steady speed command, then take about half of it.
2. Raise `Kiv` slowly until the speed rings after a change, then back off well below that. `Kiv` is an integrator:
   too much makes the motor unstable, none leaves a steady-state error.
3. Test with a speed setpoint (*Jog velocity*, or `#V 20000`; 16384 ticks per second is one revolution per
   second) and with different speeds.

A motor geared into a joint carries more inertia than a bare one and usually takes other gains; tune it in place.

### The position loop

1. Raise `Kpp` until the motor overshoots or oscillates when it reaches a target, then back off.
2. Test with a position step (*Jog position*, or `#P 16384` and `#P 0`): one revolution and back. The response
   should be quick, without overshoot; the plot shows both.

### Testing

Run the motor over the whole range of speeds and loads it will see, with a load if you can, and adjust. Then save.

## The speed estimate

The velocity loop needs the speed, which the driver estimates from the encoder count. Parameter 50 picks how:

| Parameter 50 | Estimate | How it behaves |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | moving average of the last 20 count differences | about 1.5 ms late, in steps of 312 ticks/s: the old estimate |
| 1 | PLL, the speed is its integrator | smooth, a little late |
| 2 (default) | direct PLL, integrator plus the proportional term | almost no lag, a little more noise |

Both PLLs are critically damped at the natural frequency of parameter 51, 60 Hz by default (10 to 312 Hz). The
lag of the moving average was what limited the velocity gain: on the bench the direct PLL at 60 Hz allowed 40 %
more `Kpv` before the motor vibrated, and the speed ripple was 23 to 50 % lower at 1500 to 24000 ticks/s; its
extra noise did not reach the current. Calibration and the gripper's stop detection always use the moving
average, which they were tuned with. Both parameters are not kept by Save: every power-up starts with the direct
PLL at 60 Hz. The speed in Respond_data_pack_1 and Send_Respond_Encoder_data, the watchdog descend and the capture
is the picked estimate.

## Commutation delay compensation

The voltage a control loop sets reaches the motor later than the angle it was computed from was read: the rest of
the loop, the wait for the PWM update and half a control period. By then the rotor has turned on, and the voltage
lands a little behind the angle it was meant for. Parameter 64 turns the output voltage forward by the angle the
rotor covers in that delay, in the closed-loop modes above 100 ticks/s. 166 µs is the default, measured on the
bench drive: the d-axis voltage against the cross-coupling the motor's inductance makes, at 12000 to 48000
ticks/s, fitted over 15 points. 0 switches it off; 1 to 500 µs are accepted. It is not kept by Save, so 166 µs is in
force after every power-up.

## The finer points of the velocity loop

Two settings for special cases, both off by default and not kept by Save:

- **Position input filter**, parameter 74 (Hz, 0 to 250). A host that sends positions at a fixed rate sends a
  staircase; without the speed the steps are all the loops see. The filter turns the staircase into a smooth path
  and makes its own speed from it, in position and PD modes. Use it only for a host that sends positions
  **without** the speed feedforward, at about the host's rate ÷ 12 (8 Hz for 100 Hz). On the bench it cut the
  tracking error of such a host from 1023 to 260 ticks at 12 Hz; with a host that sends the speed it made the
  tracking worse, so leave it off then.
- **Velocity-integral deadband**, parameter 75 (ticks, 0 to 2000). In position mode the velocity integral sees the
  position error less this band, so a holding motor stops pushing against a small error it cannot correct. It
  trades accuracy for holding current: on the bench 5 ticks took the holding current from 16 to 3.4 mA, and the
  mean error grew from 1.5 to 6.4 ticks.

## Impedance (PD) mode

![The impedance loop: a spring (KP) and a damper (KD) around the position setpoint, plus a current feedforward.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/PDloop.webp){ width="800" }

In PD mode the motor behaves like a spring and a damper: the current setpoint is
`KP × (setpoint − position) + KD × (speed setpoint − speed) + feedforward current`, in mA, with the position in
ticks and the speed in ticks/s. So `KP` is in mA per tick and `KD` in mA per tick/s.
Set `KP` and `KD` (the gains, or `#KP`, `#KD`, or Send_PD_Gains), then
command with `#PD`, `#PDV` and `#PDI` or Send_data_pack_PD. Start with a small `KP` and `KD` of 0, raise `KP` until
the motor holds position firmly, then add `KD` until it stops ringing. The [theory corner](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/appendix/theory/)
explains the loop.

## Limits

- The velocity limit (`#Vlimit`, 800000 by default) clamps the speed the loops may command, in encoder ticks per
  second. A rough maximum for your motor is 0.8 × V × KV × 16384 / 60 ticks per second, with KV from calibration
  and V the lower of the voltage limit and the supply voltage.
- The voltage limit (`#Vlim`) clamps the voltage of the current loops in mV. It is 6000 mV by default: a stepper's
  low resistance makes the current loop unstable with the full supply voltage, and the firmware's own guidance is
  6000 mV for a phase resistance below 2 Ω. The limit also caps the top speed. 0, or a value above the supply
  voltage, uses the supply voltage.
- `#Rstint 1` resets the integrators on every new setpoint, which avoids windup when a program sends one setpoint
  after another with large steps.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/saving/ -->

# Saving the configuration

Nothing you set survives a power cycle until you save it.

=== "Motor GUI"
    **Save**. The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you do.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Save
    ```

Saving writes the configuration to the EEPROM: the motor parameters and the calibration, every gain and limit,
the CAN node ID (and the bootloader's board ID with it), the heartbeat and watchdog settings, the thermistor and LED
settings and the gripper flag. From firmware 109 also the tool id and the watchdog fallback, the anti-cogging set
with its mode and scale, and the encoder table with its on/off switch, parameter 56 and the current-sense zero
trims. Over CAN, Send_Save_config does the same. Save after calibration, after tuning, and after changing the node
ID. The runs after a calibration save by themselves when they succeed.

Some settings are not kept and start from their defaults at every power-up: the current loop bandwidth (`#Cbw`,
160 Hz; the gains it computed are kept), the idle behaviour (`#Brake` / `#Coast` or Send_Settings: brake), the
open-loop and calibration settings (`#Openv`, `#Opens`, `#Vp`, `#Iqoffset`, `#microstep`, `#stepinterval`), and
the parameters of firmware 109 that tune the loops: the speed estimate (direct PLL at 60 Hz), the commutation delay
compensation (166 µs), the fast reading and PWM paths (on), the sin/cos table (off), the position input filter and
the velocity-integral deadband (off), the anti-cogging identification speed, the d-axis current, and the capture
and histogram settings. The [Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/defaults/) reference marks each setting, and the
[parameter table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/parameters/#every-parameter) says for every parameter whether it is kept.

!!! warning "A saved watchdog runs from power-up"
    With a watchdog saved (Send_Watchdog), the driver starts its count at power-up. A host that sends no motion
    frame or status request within the watchdog time finds the driver in watchdog error, and clears it with
    Send_Clear_Error. See [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/can/#a-control-loop).

!!! note "The serial number"
    This firmware does not read the serial number back from the EEPROM at power-up: `#SERNUM` reports 1 until it
    is set, and every save writes the value held in RAM over the stored one.

## The defaults

=== "Motor GUI"
    *Default* in the settings.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Default
    ```

Restoring the defaults writes the factory values to the EEPROM and reloads them. It also sets the thermistor to
off, resets the serial number, the hardware version and the batch date stored in the EEPROM, and clears the
gripper flag, the heartbeat rate and the watchdog; from firmware 109 also the tool id, the watchdog fallback, the
anti-cogging set, the encoder table and its zero trims, and sets parameter 56 back to its default. The CAN node ID
is kept from firmware 109 (it is 0 only when no valid ID is stored); firmware 108 and older set it to 0. Note the
hardware version and batch date `#Info` prints before you use it. The defaults are listed in the
[Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/defaults/) reference.

Use it before the first calibration of a motor, after a firmware update when the driver behaves oddly, and when
the state shows nonsense values (a `-1` where a number should be). With firmware 106 and newer that should not
happen: the driver checks the stored configuration at power-up and replaces a damaged block with the defaults by
itself.

## Where it is kept: the EEPROM

The configuration lives in an EEPROM chip on the board (a 24C16, 2 KB), apart from the firmware: flashing a new
firmware never touches it, and only the firmware's check at power-up decides to reset a part of it. Since
firmware 106 the configuration is in blocks, each with its own checksum; firmware 109 adds three:

| Block | Bytes | Checksum at | Holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| calibration | 60-188, reserved 212-236 | 208 | pole pairs, R, L, Kt, KV, flux linkage, angle offset, phase order, commutation direction, the current gains |
| settings 1 | 44-180 | 192 | CAN ID, limits, the other gains, watchdog, heartbeat, thermistor, LED, gripper flag |
| settings 2 (109) | 260-312 | 256 | tool id, watchdog fallback, the product stamp, the calibration ID; reserved slots |
| anti-cogging (109) | 324-879 | 320 | the harmonics, the table, mode and scale |
| encoder table (109) | 884-1147 | 880 | the table, its on/off switch, parameter 56, the current-sense zero trims |

At power-up a block whose checksum does not match is read again, up to three times. If it still does not match,
it gets its defaults, alone, and the others stay; a settings
reset keeps a valid CAN ID. A board saved by firmware 101 to 105, from before the checksums, is trusted when the
first 109 start finds anything it ever saved, and sealed with checksums then. The new blocks need the chip's upper
banks; on a smaller chip they keep their defaults in RAM and are not saved, which `#Info` says
(`Settings block 2: not available`, `block 3 not available`) and the identity frame's flag bit 3 shows. Going back
to an older firmware is safe: the first two blocks are unchanged, and older firmware ignores everything from byte
256 on. [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/upgrading/) says what changes when you update.

## What the driver reports

The state Motor GUI shows is what is in the EEPROM and what the driver measures. In a terminal it takes three
commands: `#Info` prints the hardware and firmware version, the CAN ID, the calibration state and the motor
parameters (pole pairs, resistance, inductance, Kt and KV), and from firmware 109 the build, the board ID and the
calibration ID, the tool id, the watchdog, the EEPROM blocks and, at its end, what is in force;
`#Param` prints the gains and limits; `#Error` the active errors.
They are the first thing to look at when something is off, and the thing to copy into a bug report.
[Status and diagnostics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/diagnostics/) explains the new lines.
