<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/errors/ -->

# Errors and recovery

When the driver detects a fault it stops the motor, goes to idle, turns the status LED on steadily and sets the
error bit in every CAN frame it sends. It stays there until the error is cleared.

## Seeing the error

- **The LED**: on and not flashing means error mode (or not calibrated). Three short flashes and a pause is
  normal operation; fast flashing is calibration.
- **`#Error`** prints `In error state!` or `No errors!`, followed by one line per active error.
- **Send_Respond_State_of_Errors** returns every flag as a bit; **the error bit** of any frame says whether there
  is one.

| Normal operation | Calibration | Error mode |
|---|---|---|
| ![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" } | ![Fast flashing during calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/Calib.webp){ width="180" } | ![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" } |

In error mode the LED does not flash: it stays on, as in the photo on the right.

## The errors

| Error | `#Error` line | Cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vbus | `Vbus error` | the supply voltage is below 9 V or above 29 V (`#Vmax`, 29000 mV after `#Default`). From firmware 109 a low voltage is not checked for the first 500 ms after power-up, while the supply ramps up | check the supply and the cable; a decelerating motor can push the voltage up |
| Encoder | `Encoder error` | the encoder reports no magnet: missing, too far away or too weak | magnet distance and type, see [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/04-mounting/magnet/) |
| Driver | `Driver error (undervoltage, thermal shutdown, or overcurrent)` | reserved: this firmware never raises it, because it does not monitor the driver stage | — |
| Velocity | `Velocity error` | the speed passed 30,000,000 ticks/s, a fixed threshold that `#Vlimit` does not change; in practice only a runaway reaches it | check the magnet and the calibration |
| Temperature | `Temp error` | the thermistor reads more than `#Tlim` (75 °C by default) or less than −20 °C, with `#Term 1`. A thermistor that is not plugged in reads far below −20 °C | let the motor cool; lower the current limit |
| E-stop | `Received ESTOP command` | Send_ESTOP was received | clear it when it is safe |
| Watchdog | `Watchdog error` | no motion frame or answered request within the watchdog time (Send_Watchdog); what the motor does then is the watchdog's action, see [The watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/watchdog/) | the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear |
| Wrong product | `Wrong firmware for this board (product lock)` | from firmware 109: this board was calibrated by the other product (a Spectral Micro firmware on a STEPFOC, or the other way round), so the firmware drives nothing ([The product lock](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/diagnostics/#the-product-lock)) | flash the right firmware; it does not clear otherwise |
| Not calibrated | `Not calibrated` | the motor has not been calibrated since `#Default`, or the EEPROM is invalid | run `#Cal` and `#Save` |
| Current | `Current error` | reserved; this firmware never raises it | — |

## Clearing

`#Clear` or Send_Clear_Error clears the flags and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes
straight back: a Vbus error at 2 V stays until the supply is right; once the supply is 24 V, one `#Clear` returns
the driver to normal operation. The calibration error clears only by calibrating (or, for a motor you know is
calibrated, `#Calibrated 1`). A gripper E-stop comes back on every control cycle until its E-stop bit is 0 again:
`#Gripstop 0`, or a Send_gripper_data_pack with the bit clear; then clear. While it is active, `#Error` prints only
`In error state!`.

## When the driver does not answer

- No LED at all: no power. Check DC+ and DC− and the cable orientation.
- LED on, no answer on UART: the baud rate (256000), TX and RX crossed, the adapter's port.
- No answer on CAN: the node ID, the termination (about 60 Ω across the bus, unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter.
- `#Info` shows `-1` or nonsense: with firmware 106 and newer this should not happen, because the driver replaces a
  damaged configuration block with the defaults at power-up. If it does, `#Default`, then calibrate again.

[Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/) goes through the symptoms one by one.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/diagnostics/ -->

# Status and diagnostics

What the driver tells about itself, from firmware 109: what is in force, who it is, its state in one frame, how
long its control loop takes, and recordings of its own signals made inside the control loop. The error flags and
what to do about each are on [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/errors/).

## What is in force

`#Info` ends with the section `In force:`, and parameter 79 holds the same as bits
([What is in force: parameter 79](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/parameters/#what-is-in-force-parameter-79)):

| Line | Says |
|---|---|
| `encoder table:` | `on, error … deg p-p`, `measured, off` or `not measured` ([Encoder table and anti-cogging](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/anti-cogging/)) |
| `anti-cogging:` | `on (harmonics)`, `on (table)`, `identified, off` or `not identified`, and `, saved` when it is the saved set |
| `current-sense zero trim:` | the two trims in counts, and whether the zero measured with the bridge switching is in use |
| `delay compensation:` | the commutation delay in µs, or `off` ([Commutation delay compensation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/#commutation-delay-compensation)) |
| `speed estimate:` | `moving average`, `PLL, … Hz` or `direct PLL, … Hz` ([The speed estimate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/#the-speed-estimate)) |
| `fast reading / fast PWM:` | the two register paths of the control loop, `on` or `off` |
| `input filter:`, `integral deadband:` | parameters 74 and 75, or `off` |
| `after #Calangle (parameter 56):` | what follows a `#Calangle`: `anti-cogging, then save` or `nothing` |
| `running:` | only while one runs: `calibration`, `encoder table`, `anti-cogging identification`, or `the runs after the calibration` |

Before that section `#Info` prints, beside what it printed before:

- `Build:` the git commit the firmware was built from, 7 hex digits. A `+` after it means it was built with
  uncommitted changes. Parameter 84 holds the same, and parameter 85 the build time in Unix seconds.
- `Board ID:` the chip's unique number, folded into 8 hex digits. It never changes. Also parameter 86.
- `Calibration ID:` a new number at every successful `#Cal`, `#Calonly` or `#Calangle`, in 8 hex digits. Save keeps
  it, and `#Default` sets it back to 0. Also parameter 87.
- `CAN RX overruns` and `CAN TX dropped`: frames the driver lost because its receive buffer was full, and answers
  it gave up after waiting 1 ms for a free transmit mailbox. Both should stay 0; they count from power-up. From
  firmware 109 the CAN controller passes only the frames addressed to the driver's own node ID, and the driver
  sends from all three transmit mailboxes, so a busy bus costs it less.
- `Product:` this firmware, STEPFOC.
- `Current sense zero:` the zeros in use, in ADC counts from 2048, measured at start-up with the bridge off (one
  count is about 1.6 mA), and what the second measurement with the bridge switching found. A zero more than 200
  counts from 2048 is not trusted: the driver then uses 2048 and says `not measured or out of range`.
  The current sensors need the motor supply. If the driver starts without it (USB plugged in before the supply),
  it waits up to half a second for the supply, then uses 2048 and says
  `no motor supply at start-up: 2048 used; measured once the supply is there`. When the supply comes, the driver
  measures the zero by itself at rest, coasting for about 80 ms even if it is set to brake, and the line shows the
  new zeros. The Vbus error the late supply latched stays until `#Clear`.
- `Tool ID`, `Watchdog: … ms, action …, fallback …`, `Settings block 2: ok` and `Anti-cogging: …, scale … %` with
  whether it is saved.

## Who the drive is: the identity frame

Send_Respond_Identity (ID 39, a remote frame) answers with the product (1 STEPFOC, 2 Spectral Micro), the tool id,
the firmware release, the hardware version, the pole pairs, whether it is calibrated, and eight flags: set up as
a gripper, brakes in idle, coils reversed, settings block 2 available, wrong product, current-sense zero measured,
anti-cogging saved, switching zero in use ([Send_Respond_Identity](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/status/#send_respond_identity)).
A host can read it before it commands or flashes a drive, to know it talks to the drive it expects.

The **tool id** says what the drive is built into: 0 none (a joint or a bare driver), 1 an SSG-48, 11 to 33 an
MSG (the tens digit the rail, 1 = 100, 2 = 150, 3 = 200 mm; the units digit the stepper, 1 = 21.5, 2 = 40,
3 = 60 mm), 200 to 254 your own tools. Set it with `#Tool` or parameter 1 and save.

## Everything at once: telemetry

Send_Respond_Telemetry (ID 40, a remote frame) answers with the temperature, the supply voltage, both error bytes
and the current, all from the same moment: one request instead of four, for a host that watches many drives
([Send_Respond_Telemetry](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/status/#send_respond_telemetry)).

## The product lock

STEPFOC and the Spectral Micro use the same bootloader and the same file name for their firmware, and each
firmware drives the other board wrongly: the Spectral firmware on a STEPFOC drove a coil at about 1.7 A in every
mode on the bench. From firmware 109 a board remembers which product calibrated it, a stamp in the EEPROM written
at the first start-up of a calibrated board and at every save. A firmware that finds the other product's stamp,
or no stamp but a calibration its own product cannot make (STEPFOC calibrates only 50, 75, 100 or 125 pole pairs),
reads and writes nothing more, drives no pin and starts no control loop. It stays reachable: it reports an error,
`Wrong firmware for this board (product lock)` in `#Error`, the `wrong_product` bit in the error state and the
identity, and a warning in `#Info`. Flash the right firmware and the board runs as before; nothing was written.

`#Product` shows the stamp. On a board the rule misjudges, `#Product claim` stamps it as this product and
`#Product clear` removes the stamp; power-cycle after either. Both are UART commands only.

## How long the control loop takes

The control loop runs every 160 µs (6250 Hz) and has to finish inside that. `#Info` prints the last loop's time;
parameters 66 to 70 give its five sections, averaged over about 64 loops, in 0.1 µs: the checks, reading the
encoder, the currents and the supply, the transforms, the control mode with the PWM, and the rest (the capture).

On the bench drive with everything on (anti-cogging, delay compensation, the direct PLL, the encoder table, fast
reading and PWM) the loop took about 129 µs of its 160 while the motor turned, 128 µs while it held, 68 µs in
idle. What the features cost while turning:

| Feature | Parameter | µs per loop |
|---|---|---|
| anti-cogging on | 37 | about 10 |
| commutation delay compensation | 64 | about 10 |
| encoder table on | 53 | 0.1 |
| moving average instead of the direct PLL | 50 | −1 |
| sin and cos from the table | 65 | +1.3 (slower, so off) |
| fast reading off | 71 | +14 |
| fast PWM off | 72 | +4 |

Without the two fast paths the loop would take about 148 µs while turning, too close to 160 for comfort: leave
them on. They read the ADC and the encoder and write the PWM by register instead of through the library calls,
with every wait bounded; the current noise stayed the same.

## A capture

The capture records three signals inside the control loop, sample by sample, 1024 samples per channel: what the
loop saw and did, which a host polling over the bus cannot see. Parameters 24 to 33 set it up and report on it,
Send_Buffer_Read with kind 0 reads it ([Reading the capture](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/parameters/#reading-the-capture);
the signals are listed under [Capture and histogram](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/parameters/#capture-and-histogram)).
While the encoder table or the anti-cogging run turns the motor, a capture is not armed: the runs use its memory.

A step response, 1024 samples of speed, current and position error, one every 2 loops (0.33 s):

```python
import time
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral

comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

def read_all(seconds):
    end = time.time() + seconds
    while time.time() < end:
        message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.01)
        if message is not None:
            motor.UnpackData(message, ids)

for number, value in ((24, 4), (25, 1), (26, 7), (27, 2), (28, 1)):
    motor.Send_Parameter(number, value)     # A speed, B Iq, C position error; every 2nd loop; start now
motor.Send_data_pack_1(1000, 0, 0)          # the step: to position 1000
read_all(0.5)
motor.Send_Get_Parameter(32)                # how many samples
read_all(0.1)
count = motor.parameters.get(32, 0)
motor.Send_Buffer_Read(0, 0, count)         # kind 0, from sample 0
read_all(3.0)
for i in sorted(motor.capture):
    speed, iq, position_error = motor.capture[i]
    print(i, speed, iq, position_error)
```

Trigger 2 records up to an error instead: armed with a pre-trigger, it keeps the moments before a trip, the
watchdog's included, and the time after it. The capture calls (`Send_Parameter`, `Send_Get_Parameter`,
`Send_Buffer_Read`) need the Spectral-BLDC library 1.21 or newer.

## Memory

The drive's microcontroller has 128 KB of flash, of which the bootloader takes 12 KB, and 20 KB of RAM. Firmware
109 uses about 91 % of the 116 KB application flash and 65 % of the RAM for fixed data, which leaves about
7 KB for the stack and the heap. Parameter 83 (`#Par 83`, or Send_Get_Parameter(83)) is the margin check: the
bytes of that RAM the stack has never reached since start-up. The stack needs about 1.5 to 2 KB; read parameter 83
after the drive has run its hardest work (a calibration, the encoder table, the anti-cogging, sound) and see that
plenty is left.

## A histogram

The histogram adds one signal into 256 bins over the electrical angle or over one motor turn, every control loop,
until it is stopped or a bin holds 65535 samples (about 45 minutes): the mean per bin shows what repeats with the
angle, such as the cogging current at a steady speed. Parameter 35 picks the signal, 34 starts it (1 electrical
angle, 2 motor turn) and stops it (0), 36 counts the samples, and Send_Buffer_Read with kind 1 reads the count and
the sum of each bin. The anti-cogging identification uses it the same way; while it runs, parameters 34 and 35
refuse a write.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/sound/ -->

# Sound

From firmware 109 the driver plays sound through its motor: tones, chords, tunes from a queue it plays by itself,
and recorded sound such as speech. A current at an audio frequency in the windings makes a small force at that
frequency, and the motor, and above all whatever it is fixed to, radiate it as sound.

## How it works

- **Where:** the driver adds the sound to its output voltage, after the current loop. By default it goes on the q
  axis (parameter 82 = 1), where it makes torque: the rotor rocks at the tone's pitch. On the bench that was much
  louder than the d axis (82 = 0), which makes no torque at all.
- **When:** only while the driver holds or moves: position, velocity, current or PD mode. Idle, or any error,
  stops all sound. A joint keeps holding its pose while it plays.
- **Tones:** up to 4 at once (channels 0 to 3), a chord on one motor, each with its own pitch, loudness and length.
- **Loudness** is given as a current, in mA. The coil's impedance rises with the pitch (√(R² + (2πfL)²), from the
  motor's R and L), so the same voltage would sound much quieter high than low; the driver turns the current into
  the voltage that pitch needs, and a note is as loud low as high.
- **Pitch:** 20 Hz up to just below 3125 Hz, half the 6250 Hz control loop. Tones are clean up to about a third of
  the loop rate; melodies sit well between C4 and C6 (262 to 1047 Hz).
- **The queue:** 31 events, each setting one channel's pitch and loudness and then waiting. The control loop plays
  them with loop-exact timing, so the host's own timing never reaches the music: it loads the queue and starts it.
- **Samples:** recorded sound, 8 bits, played from a 1024-place buffer at a rate the host sets, up to the loop
  rate. Speech comes through recognisable but muffled: the telephone band reaches 3400 Hz, the motor about 3 kHz.
- **The cap:** all sound together is limited to the voltage of parameter 81, 2000 mV by default; 0 refuses sound.
  None of the sound settings is saved.

## A tone over UART

```
#Tone 440,250,1000      440 Hz, 250 mA, 1000 ms
#Tone 880,200,0         until stopped
#Tone off               stops all sound
```

From idle, a calibrated driver first holds the position it is at and says so (`Holding the position while it
plays (#Idle releases it)`); `#Idle` releases it afterwards. Left out, the loudness is 200 mA and the length
500 ms. `Tone: not played` means the driver is not calibrated or in an error, the pitch is outside 20 Hz to half the
loop rate, or parameter 81 is 0.

## Over CAN and from Python

Send_Sound (ID 44) carries every operation: a tone now, an event for the queue, play the queue, play the samples,
stop. Send_Sound_Samples (ID 45) fills the sample buffer ([Sound](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/sound/) in the CAN
reference). The Python calls below need the Spectral-BLDC library 1.21 or newer, as does its `music` module (note
names, ringtone melodies, MIDI files, WAV files).

Over CAN the host makes the driver hold first, for example with a position frame to where the motor is:

```python
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
from Spectral_BLDC import music

comms = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM41', bitrate=1000000)
motor = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=comms)

def read_answers(seconds=0.1):
    message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=seconds)
    while message is not None:
        motor.UnpackData(message, ids)
        message, ids = comms.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.005)

motor.Send_Respond_Encoder_data()                # where the motor is
read_answers()
motor.Send_data_pack_1(motor.position, 0, 0)     # hold it there
read_answers()

motor.Send_Tone(440, current_mA=250, duration_ms=1000)        # one tone
for channel, note in enumerate(('C4', 'E4', 'G4')):            # a chord: three channels at once
    motor.Send_Tone(music.note_hz(note), current_mA=200, duration_ms=1500, channel=channel)
```

A tune goes into the queue and plays by itself. A melody becomes two events per note (the note, then a short
silence, so repeated notes are heard as two), so up to 15 notes fit at once:

```python
name, melody = music.parse_rtttl('scale:d=8,o=5,b=120:c,d,e,f,g,a,b,c6')
for channel, freq, current, wait in music.melody_events(melody, current_mA=250):
    motor.Send_Sound_Event(freq, current, wait, channel=channel)
motor.Send_Sound_Play()
```

For a longer tune, keep loading events while it plays: bits 0 to 7 of parameter 80 say how many are still
queued. `music.read_midi` reads a MIDI file, `music.split_voices` splits it into lines for the four channels, and
`music.lines_events` makes the queue's events from them.

Recorded sound: convert a WAV file to samples at the rate the motor plays, fill the buffer, start it, and keep it
filled:

```python
rate = 3125
samples = music.wav_samples('hello.wav', rate, coil_tau_s=0.0026 / 1.1, clip_percentile=0.95)
motor.Send_Samples(samples[:1000])               # fill the buffer first
motor.Send_Samples_Play(rate, full_scale_mV=2000)
sent = 1000
while sent < len(samples):
    motor.Send_Get_Parameter(80)
    read_answers(0.02)
    buffered = (motor.parameters.get(80, 0) >> 8) & 0x7FF
    room = 1000 - buffered
    if room > 0:
        motor.Send_Samples(samples[sent:sent + room])
        sent += room
```

`coil_tau_s` is the coil's L ÷ R (here 2.6 mH and 1.1 Ω): the function raises the high frequencies the coil
would otherwise swallow, and `clip_percentile` levels speech so that it plays about four times louder. At 3125
samples a second a driver takes about 391 frames a second, some 5 % of the bus. When the buffer runs dry the
playing stops and bit 27 of parameter 80 says so.

Send_Sound and Send_Sound_Samples do not reset the watchdog: with a watchdog set, keep sending a status request
while the sound plays.

## Limits and care

- **Fix the motor to something that rings.** A box or a table is far louder than a motor in free air, and a loose
  motor jumps and distorts the sound. On the bench a bare NEMA 17 was taped down.
- **Keep tones short and moderate.** `#Tone` and Send_Tone default to 200 mA; the bench played notes at 250 mA.
  The sound current comes on top of the holding current and heats the motor like any other current; a motor is
  made to turn, and long loud tones are hard on it.
- **On the q axis a tone is a small torque ripple:** a held joint vibrates slightly at the tone's pitch. Choose the
  d axis (parameter 82 = 0) when that matters; it is quieter.
- **The cap**, parameter 81, limits all sound together; the output also clamps at the supply voltage.

On the bench (2026-11-08, STEPFOC, a bare NEMA 17 taped down), tones, scales, a tune from the queue, four-note
chords and streamed speech all played. The q axis was much louder than the d axis, speech was audible but
muffled, and there were no errors, no warming and only small vibrations.

## The arm as an instrument

Every joint of a robot can play its own line, and because the sound rides on top of the control, the arm keeps
holding its pose while it plays. Load each driver's queue first, then start them one after another: the starts
are meant to fall within about a millisecond of each other, and from then on each driver keeps its own time
(whether they stay together over a whole song is still to be measured). Split a MIDI file
into as many lines as there are channels, four per driver, and give each driver its four. Through a gearbox the
sound changes with the joint; try each joint's range. Playing on an assembled arm has not been tested yet.

## Checking what plays

| Parameter | Says |
|---|---|
| 79, bit 24 | sound is playing |
| 80 | bits 0-7 events queued, 8-18 samples buffered, 24 a tone sounds, 25 the queue plays, 26 samples play, 27 the samples ran dry |
| 81 | the sound's voltage cap, mV |
| 82 | the axis: 1 q, 0 d |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/gripper-mode/ -->

# Gripper mode

A driver can run a gripper instead of a joint: the same board, with a state machine that moves a jaw to a
position between open and closed, at a speed, with a current limit that becomes the grip force, and that reports
when it holds something. The [MSG gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/) is built on
STEPFOC this way.

## Turning it on

```
#Gripper 1
#Save
```

`#Default` clears the flag again. A driver in gripper mode still answers every other command; the gripper
commands only work with the flag set.

## Calibrating the gripper

After every power-up the gripper has to find its end stops: `#Gripcal` or Send_gripper_calibrate. The jaws open
until they stop, then close until they stop, slowly and at 500 mA; the positions become 0 (open) and 255 (closed).
The driver prints nothing when it is done. If it has not found both end stops within about 24 s it gives up, and
the gripper stays uncalibrated. Check the result with `#Gripinfo` (`Gripper calibrated is: 1`) or the
`gripper_calibrated` bit of Respond_Gripper_data_pack: a move is carried out only once the gripper is calibrated.
The motor itself must be calibrated (`#Cal`) and saved before that, once.

While the gripper calibrates, send only empty status polls. A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error
or `#Clear` stops the calibration without a message, and the next one then starts part way through, where the
stopped one left off: switch the driver off and on before you calibrate again
([known issue KI-7](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/)).

## Moving

Over UART:

```
#Gripvel 100       speed, 0 to 255
#Gripcur 400       current limit of the move in mA, the grip force
#Grippos 200       go to position 200 (0 open, 255 closed); also activates the gripper
```

Over CAN, Send_gripper_data_pack carries position, speed and current in one frame with the activate and action
bits; the driver answers with Respond_Gripper_data_pack: the position, the measured current, whether it is moving,
and the object detection:

| Object detection | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | moving |
| 1 | an object was detected while closing: the jaws stopped on it and hold it with the current limit |
| 2 | an object was detected while opening |
| 3 | the position was reached |

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack (0 bytes) only asks for the state. The answer to a 5-byte command goes out
before the driver acts on it, so its object detection and error bits are still those of the moment before
(KI-6); the answers to the next frames show the new move. The action bit in the answer is a copy of the last
command's action bit and stays 1 after the move ends (KI-8): the object detection tells when it has ended.

Send_gripper_data_pack's E-stop bit raises the
gripper E-stop error; `#Gripstop 1` does the same over UART. The error stays: while the E-stop bit is 1 the driver
raises it again on every control cycle, and `#Error` prints only `In error state!`. To recover, clear the bit
(`#Gripstop 0`, or a Send_gripper_data_pack with the bit 0), then `#Clear` or Send_Clear_Error.

!!! warning "Current"
    From firmware 109 a gripper move uses the magnitude of the current you give it, at most the driver's
    2800 mA; 108 and older used it as sent. The safe range depends on the gripper's mechanics and motor; the
    gripper's manual gives it.

## Where the details are

The bytes of the two gripper frames are in the [CAN reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/gripper/), the UART commands in
the [UART reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/uart/gripper/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/ -->

# Firmware

The driver's firmware is open source and released as numbered builds. A driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer
carries a bootloader and updates itself over UART or CAN, and so do some drivers shipped before 105, which report
103 ([Drivers that report 103](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/releases/#drivers-that-report-103) says how to tell). A driver without the
bootloader needs it installed once with a programming adapter.

## In this chapter

- [Releases and versions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/releases/): how releases are numbered, how to see which one a driver runs, what the
  release notes contain
- [The bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/the-bootloader/): what it is, how the driver boots, how it is entered, its protocol and tools
- [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/): the normal update, with Motor GUI, the bootloader's command-line
  tool, or a PAR6 control box
- [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/upgrading/): what a driver keeps when it is updated to this release, what works
  at once and what has to be run
- [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/): for a driver that runs firmware 103 or older
- [Building from source](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/building/): PlatformIO, the memory layout, uploading with a programming adapter

The release notes of every release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix,
[Firmware release notes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/appendix/firmware-release-notes/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/releases/ -->

# Releases and versions

A firmware release is a number: 103, 105, 106, … Every release is a tag `V<number>` in the
[firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller) and a GitHub release that
carries the image `stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin`, a manifest `firmware.json` with the image's size, SHA-256 and
the commit it was built from, and the release notes. The notes are the firmware's changelog; the
[appendix](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/appendix/firmware-release-notes/) collects them.

## Which release does my driver run?

```
#Info
```

prints `Software version: <number>` among the rest; Motor GUI shows the same number in the driver's identity, and
over CAN Send_Respond_Device_Info returns it as the third byte. From firmware 109 Send_Respond_Identity returns it
too, as a 16-bit number, with the product it was built for. From firmware 105 the number is the build's own
version. Before that it was read from the EEPROM, where the last `#Default` wrote it, so it names the firmware
that last restored the defaults, not necessarily the one running: 101 and 102 write 101, 103 writes 103.

### Drivers that report 103

A driver that reports 103 runs either release 103 from the `main` branch, without a bootloader, or an early build
of the `bootloader-version` branch, which also writes 103 and runs above the bootloader. Some drivers were shipped
with the bootloader before release 105. Which image those carry was not recorded: most likely 103, built for
the bootloader.

To tell whether yours has the bootloader:

- Watch the LED as you switch the driver on: with the bootloader it blinks for about two seconds before the
  firmware starts.
- Or power it up while `bl_flash.py list` or Motor GUI's *Scan bootloaders* is polling: a driver with the
  bootloader answers in its first two seconds.

With the bootloader, update it to the current release as in [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/); the
release it ran before does not matter then. Without one, install it first:
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/).

## Which release does this site describe?

The one in the version box on the [landing page](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/) and in the version selector in the header. When a
newer release changes what a page says, a new version of the site is published and the previous one stays
reachable from the selector. The [compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/appendix/compatibility/) says which releases go with
which bootloader, Python library and PAR6 runtime.

## The Spectral Micro counterpart

A change that applies to both drivers comes to the Spectral Micro too. From release 109 the two drivers share
their version numbers and are released together (the Spectral Micro went from 107 straight to 109; there is no
Spectral Micro 108). Before, the numbers did not always match: STEPFOC 108 went with Spectral Micro 107. The
compatibility table lists the pairs.

## The two branches

Releases from 105 on are built from the `bootloader-version` branch of the repository, whose firmware is linked
to run above the bootloader. The `main` branch holds the firmware of release 103 and earlier, linked to run
without a bootloader, and is not updated. A board running 103 is documented by version `103` of this site; to
move it to a current release, see [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/the-bootloader/ -->

# The bootloader

Every driver shipped with firmware 105 or newer carries a small bootloader in the first 12 KB of its flash. It
starts the firmware on a normal boot, and it loads a new firmware over UART or CAN when a host asks, so a driver is
updated without a programming adapter and without opening anything. The bootloader is open source:
[stm32f103c-bootloader](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader), shared with the Spectral Micro.

## Memory layout

| Address | Contents |
|---|---|
| `0x08000000` – `0x080022FF` | the bootloader (about 9 KB) |
| `0x08002C00` – `0x08002FFF` | the bootloader's configuration page: the board ID, the firmware's page count and CRC, the bootloader's build version |
| `0x08003000` – `0x0801FFFF` | the firmware (up to 116 KB) |
| RAM `0x20001000` | a magic word the bootloader sets to hand over to the firmware |

The firmware is linked to start at `0x08003000` and sets its vector table there (`VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000`); the
first `0x3000` bytes belong to the bootloader and the firmware never touches them.

## What happens at boot

1. On a reset, the bootloader runs first. If the magic word is in RAM and the reset was a software reset, it
   checks the firmware's stack pointer and reset vector and jumps straight into the firmware: about 10 ms, the
   normal boot.
2. Otherwise it initialises the clocks, CAN, UART and its watchdog, and **listens for a host for 2 s**. The LED
   flashes three times at the start, then blinks while the bootloader listens, faster while a host talks to it.
3. With no host, and a firmware whose stored CRC is valid, it sets the magic word and resets; the next boot takes
   the fast path.
4. With a host talking, it stays as long as the host keeps talking: 3 s after the last command, 60 s once a flash
   is in progress. Any `PING` resets the timer.
5. With no valid firmware (never flashed, or a flash that was interrupted), it stays in bootloader mode and waits,
   with the LED blinking; the driver answers nothing on `#Info`.

## Entering the bootloader

- **From the firmware**: `#Reset` over UART or Send_Reset (command 14) over CAN. Since firmware 105 both reset
  the driver into the bootloader's 2 s window; the host tools send them for you.
- **At power-on**: the 2 s window after every power-up, if the host is already polling.
- **Always**, when there is no valid firmware.

## The board ID

The bootloader has a board ID of its own, 0 to 13, stored in its configuration page. 14 and 15 do not exist
for it: its command frame, identifier `0x700`, decodes as node 14 in the firmware's identifier scheme, so those
two node IDs are reserved. **Give drivers node IDs 0 to 13.** The firmware accepts `#CANID 14` and `15`, but the
bootloader then keeps its old board ID and a firmware update over CAN cannot reach the driver. The firmware keeps
the board ID in step with its CAN node ID when the configuration is saved: `#Save` or Send_Save_config writes the
node ID into the bootloader's board ID, so a driver answers the host tools under its node ID. A node ID that is set
but not saved is not the board ID yet. A
replacement board ships as ID 0; two boards with the same ID on one bus corrupt each other's flash stream, so
give the new board its ID alone on the bus first (`set-id` in the host tool).

## Transports and protocol

Over **CAN** (1 Mbit/s, standard 11-bit identifiers) the host commands on identifier `0x700` with 8 data bytes
(`board_id`, `cmd`, two parameters); the board replies on `0x701 + board_id` with 5 bytes (`board_id`, `cmd`,
error code, a 16-bit parameter); the firmware image streams in bulk frames on `(board_id << 7) | sequence`,
16 frames of 8 bytes per chunk, with no reply per frame. Over **UART** (256000 baud) the same commands travel in
framed packets `[0xBB][CMD][LEN][BOARD_ID][DATA…][CRC16]` with the same 5-byte reply, but the first four have other
numbers.

Commands over CAN: `WBUF` (1), `WPAGE` (2), `WCRC` (3), `PING` (4), `SET_ID` (5), `ERASE_APP` (6),
`STREAM_BEGIN` (7), `STREAM_STATUS` (8). Over UART: `PING` (1), `WBUF` (2), `WPAGE` (3), `WCRC` (4), and the
others as over CAN, plus `STREAM_DATA` (9), which carries the stream frames. Error codes: `0` OK, `1` invalid offset, `2` invalid CRC, `3` flash write failed, `4` invalid
page number. A flash is: ping, reset the firmware if it answers, ping until the bootloader answers, `ERASE_APP`
(about 3.5 s), then for each 1 KB page `STREAM_BEGIN`, 8 chunks of 16 frames, `STREAM_STATUS`, `WPAGE` with the
page's CRC32; finally `WCRC` with the page count and the image's CRC32. The bootloader stores the CRC and
reboots into the new firmware. The full wire protocol is in the bootloader repository's `docs/PROTOCOL.md`.

## The host side

| Tool | Transport | Use |
|---|---|---|
| [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/motor-gui/) | serial adapter (Web Serial) or CANvas | one driver on the bench, releases fetched from GitHub |
| `host_tools/bl_flash.py` in the bootloader repository | slcan or gs_usb CAN adapters, or UART | scripts, several boards, `list`, `set-id`, `flash --erase-first` |
| the PAR6 control box's `flash_motor_firmware.py` and the dashboard's Firmware tab | the robot's own CAN bus | every joint of a robot, from the box |

[Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/) has the commands.

## Recovery

An interrupted flash leaves an invalid CRC; the bootloader refuses to start the firmware and waits, so the board is
not lost: flash again. A board that answers nothing at all: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch
the 2 s window. The one thing the tools refuse, and that would need a programming adapter to undo, is flashing an
image linked for `0x08000000` (a firmware from the `main` branch) over the firmware region.

## Installing it

Boards that run release 103 or older from the `main` branch have no bootloader; some boards shipped before 105
have it although they report 103 ([Drivers that report 103](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/releases/#drivers-that-report-103)).
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/)
puts it there once, with a programming adapter at `0x08000000`; from then on the board updates like any other.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/ -->

# Updating through the bootloader

A driver with the bootloader (firmware 105 or newer) is updated over the UART connector or the CAN bus: the host
tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image into it.
No programming adapter, and nothing to open.

!!! warning "Before you update"
    - Park the mechanism: the motor loses torque during the update and until the new firmware is calibrated and
      commanded.
    - An update may clear the calibration (the release notes say so when it does); plan to calibrate and `#Save`
      afterwards, and note the gains `#Info` prints. An update to 109 keeps it:
      [Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/upgrading/) says what changes and what to run.
    - On a bus with several drivers, update each node; a bus with mixed releases behaves unpredictably.

## With Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) in Chrome or Edge, connected over the serial adapter or the CANvas adapter:
choose the release, and the GUI fetches the image and its manifest from the GitHub release, verifies the size and
the SHA-256, resets the driver into its bootloader and flashes it. This is the way for one driver on the bench.

## With the bootloader's command-line tool

The [bootloader repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader) has `host_tools/bl_flash.py`,
which flashes an image over CAN (slcan or candleLight/gs_usb adapters) or over UART:

=== "Windows"
    ```
    cd host_tools
    pip install -r requirements.txt

    # over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter on COM6, driver with board ID 0
    python bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel COM6 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

    # over UART on COM7
    python bl_flash.py --transport uart --port COM7 --baudrate 256000 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
    ```

=== "Linux"
    ```
    cd host_tools
    pip install -r requirements.txt

    # over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/ttyACM0 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

    # over UART with the serial adapter
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baudrate 256000 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
    ```
    Your user needs the `dialout` group for both ports ([Motor GUI: the port](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/motor-gui/#opening-the-port)).

=== "macOS"
    ```
    cd host_tools
    pip install -r requirements.txt

    # over CAN with a CANvas (slcan) adapter, driver with board ID 0; ls /dev/cu.usbmodem* gives the name
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport can --can-interface slcan --channel /dev/cu.usbmodem1101 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first

    # over UART with the serial adapter; ls /dev/cu.usbserial* gives the name
    python3 bl_flash.py --transport uart --port /dev/cu.usbserial-0001 --baudrate 256000 flash stepfoc-firmware-V109.bin --board 0 --erase-first
    ```

The tool sends the reset command to the running firmware (`#Reset` over UART, Send_Reset over CAN), catches the
bootloader's two-second window, erases the application pages and streams the image page by page, each page
verified by a CRC; `list` shows the boards in bootloader mode, `set-id` changes a board's bootloader ID. The image
is the `stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin` from the GitHub release.

!!! note "Board ID and node ID"
    The bootloader has its own board ID (0 to 13), kept in its configuration page, separate from the firmware's
    CAN node ID. The firmware keeps the two in step when the configuration is saved (`#Save`, Send_Save_config),
    so a driver's bootloader ID is normally its node ID. After `#CANID`, save before you flash over CAN.

!!! success "Check"
    After the flash, from Motor GUI or the tool, the driver starts the new firmware: `#Info` prints the release
    you flashed as `Software version`, and Motor GUI shows it in the driver's identity. If the driver does not
    answer, see [When it fails](#when-it-fails).

## From a PAR6 control box

A robot built on the Robot Control Box updates every joint from the box itself, over its own CAN bus, from the
dashboard's Firmware tab or with `tools/flash_motor_firmware.py`; the
[PAR6 documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/par6/) describes it.

## What happens in the driver

1. The host sends the reset; the firmware reboots into the bootloader.
2. The bootloader listens for two seconds. With no host it starts the firmware; with a host it stays as long as
   the host keeps talking (60 s during a flash).
3. The application pages are erased, then written page by page; each page is checked by a CRC.
4. The bootloader checks the whole image's CRC, records it, and starts the new firmware.

## When it fails

A flash that fails or is cancelled part way is not a brick: the stored CRC is invalid, so the bootloader refuses to
start the firmware and waits for a host. Run the flash again; `bl_flash.py list` (or a passive scan from the
control box) finds the board. A board that answers nothing: power-cycle it with the host already polling, to catch
the two-second window.

An image linked for `0x08000000` (a firmware from the `main` branch, release 103 and earlier) must never be
flashed through the bootloader: it would overwrite the bootloader's own region if the tool did not refuse it.
The tools validate the image first.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/upgrading/ -->

# Upgrading from older firmware

Firmware 109 changes how the driver measures and controls the motor more than any release before it. This page
says what a driver keeps when it is updated to 109, what works at once, what has to be run, and how to go back.
[Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/) is how to flash it.

## What is kept

Flashing never touches the EEPROM, where the configuration lives
([Where it is kept](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/saving/#where-it-is-kept-the-eeprom)). A driver updated from 106, 107 or 108
starts with everything it had:

- the calibration: pole pairs, R, L, the angle offset, Kt, KV, the phase order and direction;
- the CAN ID, the gains, the limits, the watchdog, the heartbeat, the thermistor and the gripper settings.

A driver from 101 to 105, saved before the configuration had checksums, is trusted and sealed at its first start
of 109 when it was ever saved; 108 reset a board saved but never calibrated, CAN ID included, and 109 keeps it.
Release 103 and older from the `main` branch have no bootloader: such a board needs the programming adapter once
([Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/)).

The new settings start from their defaults: tool id 0, the watchdog fallback 2000 ms / 0 mA / 1000 ticks/s / legacy,
parameter 56 = 2.

## What works at once

These need no measurement and are on from the first start of 109:

- the **direct PLL speed estimate** at 60 Hz ([The speed estimate](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/#the-speed-estimate));
- **commutation delay compensation**, 166 µs ([Commutation delay compensation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/#commutation-delay-compensation));
- the **fast reading and PWM** paths of the control loop;
- the **current-sense zero**, measured at every start-up: a STEPFOC that read about 48 mA of current with nothing
  flowing reads under 1 mA;
- undervoltage is not checked for the first 500 ms after power-up, so a supply that ramps up slowly no longer
  leaves a Vbus error behind (overvoltage always is);
- the **watchdog actions**: the action byte the host already sends is acted on. Byte 0, what the Python library and
  the PAR6 runtime send, gives the legacy response, so an unchanged host sees no difference;
- `#Default` and a settings reset **keep the CAN ID**;
- the new CAN commands and parameters, the identity frame, telemetry, the capture, `#Info`'s `In force:`, and
  [sound through the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/sound/).

## What has to be run

These are off after the update, because nothing is saved for them yet; the encoder table and the anti-cogging
cannot be switched on before they are measured:

- the **encoder table**;
- the **anti-cogging**;
- the **current-sense zero trim**.

A calibration runs all three ([What follows the calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/#what-follows-the-calibration));
so does `#Encal all` without a calibration.

## What does not change by itself

- **The current gains.** The saved Kpiq and Kiiq stay as they are: on a driver calibrated before 109 they are the
  old gains divided by 7, a loop of about 70 Hz (parameter 49 reads about 71). A calibration computes them again
  at 160 Hz; so does `#Cbw 160` (or parameter 49 = 160), then `#Save`.
- **The velocity gains.** The saved Kpv and Kiv stay as they are, typically 0.007 and 0.0005. Firmware 109 was
  tuned with 0.02 and 0.001, the PLL speed estimate allowing the higher gain; set them yourself
  ([The velocity loop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/#the-velocity-loop)).

## The whole upgrade

1. Flash 109 ([Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/)). `#Info` prints `Software version: 109` and ends with
   `In force:`.
2. Check that the current limit suits the motor (`#Ilim`), then calibrate, with the shaft free: `#Cal`. The
   encoder table (at 80 % of the current limit), the anti-cogging and the trim follow, and everything is saved
   (about two minutes in all).
3. Set the velocity gains, for example `#Kpv 0.02` and `#Kiv 0.001` (a 21.5 mm stepper overshot 95 % at these on
   the bench; its presets use `#Kpv 0.014` and `#Kiv 0.00014`), then `#Save`. (Calibration puts the
   current limit that was in force back when it ends; set `#Ilim` for your motor before step 2 if it is not.)
4. Check `#Info`: `encoder table: on`, `anti-cogging: on (harmonics), saved`.

With Motor GUI's presets: apply the preset first, then calibrate, then set the velocity gains. On firmware 109 a
preset writes the current gains of a 160 Hz loop for its own R and L, the same a calibration computes from them,
and its own velocity gains.

On a robot whose joints cannot turn freely, neither the calibration nor the runs after it can be made in place.
There skip step 2: the drive keeps the calibration it has, the new speed estimate, the delay compensation and the
current-sense zero work at once, and `#Cbw 160` with `#Save` gives the new current gains. The encoder table and
the anti-cogging then stay off.

## Going back

Flashing 108 or older over 109 is safe for the configuration: the calibration and the first settings block are
unchanged, and older firmware ignores everything 109 saved from byte 256 on (tool id, fallback, anti-cogging,
encoder table). Flash 109 again and they are all still there.

!!! note "Not yet tested on the bench"
    The upgrade from 103 (programming adapter, then the bootloader, then 109) and a downgrade to 108 had not been
    tested on the bench when this page was written; the rest of what it says was, except where the pages it links
    say otherwise.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/ -->

# Installing the bootloader on an older board

A driver running release 103 or older from the `main` branch has no bootloader: its firmware starts at the
beginning of the flash. A driver that reports 103 may have the bootloader all the same; check first, as in
[Drivers that report 103](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/releases/#drivers-that-report-103). To
run any release from 105 on, which is linked to start above the bootloader, the bootloader must be installed
once, with a programming adapter on the JTAG connector. After that, every update goes over UART or CAN.

!!! warning
    Disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter before connecting the programming adapter. The adapter
    powers the board at 3.3 V.

## What you need

- The [programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/jtag-programming-adapter-1-27-pitch) (an ST-LINK
  with the 1.27 mm pogo-pin adapter for the JTAG pads), or any ST-LINK, J-Link or OpenOCD-compatible probe wired
  to 3.3 V, GND, SWDIO and SWCLK.
- [STM32CubeProgrammer](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeprog.html) or the older
  [STM32 ST-LINK Utility](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stsw-link004.html) on the PC, with the
  [ST-LINK drivers](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stsw-link009.html).
- The bootloader binary from the [bootloader repository's `bin/` folder](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/stm32f103c-bootloader/tree/main/bin);
  its `README.md` names the current file.

=== "Windows"
    STM32CubeProgrammer or the ST-LINK Utility, and the ST-LINK USB driver (STSW-LINK009) for the adapter.

=== "Linux"
    STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver, but your user
    needs access to its USB device: install the udev rules that come with STM32CubeProgrammer, or run it with
    `sudo`.

=== "macOS"
    STM32CubeProgrammer; the ST-LINK Utility runs on Windows only. The adapter needs no driver.

![The JTAG pads, marked 3V3, GND, SWCLK, SWDIO. The adapter is pressed onto them; a little pressure makes the contact.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/STEPFOC_JTAG.webp){ width="700" }

## Steps

1. Connect the adapter to the JTAG pads and the PC.
2. In the programmer, connect to the target (SWD). The STM32F103CB shows up with 128 KB of flash.
3. Erase the chip, or at least the application region: the old firmware and the bootloader must not overlap.
4. Program the bootloader binary at address **`0x08000000`**.
5. Disconnect the adapter, power the driver. The bootloader finds no valid application and waits in bootloader
   mode, with the LED blinking.
6. Flash the firmware release through the bootloader, over UART or CAN, as in
   [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/).
7. `#Info` shows the new release. `#Default`, enter the motor parameters, calibrate, `#Save`.

!!! success "Check"
    `#Info` prints the release you flashed, and a driver powered up while `bl_flash.py list` or Motor GUI's
    *Scan bootloaders* is polling answers in its first two seconds: the bootloader is there. If the firmware does
    not start, see [Updating through the bootloader: when it fails](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/#when-it-fails).

!!! note "Memory layout"
    `0x08000000`–`0x080022FF` bootloader, `0x08002C00` its configuration page (board ID, the application's CRC),
    `0x08003000`–`0x0801FFFF` the application (116 KB). The bootloader keeps a magic value in RAM to hand over
    to the application in about 10 ms on a normal boot.

## The programmer's settings

In ST-LINK Utility, *Target → Settings* with SWD and the default frequency works; *Target → Program & Verify*
with the start address `0x08000000`. The pictures of the old flashing procedure apply to the connection and the
settings dialog:

| Settings | Programming |
|---|---|
| ![ST-LINK settings](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/stlink1.webp){ width="420" } | ![ST-LINK program and verify](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/stlink_prog.webp){ width="420" } |

The same adapter uploads a firmware you build yourself, see [Building from source](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/building/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/building/ -->

# Building from source

The firmware is a PlatformIO project for the Arduino core on the STM32F103CB, in the `STEPFOC firmware` folder
of the [firmware repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/bootloader-version/STEPFOC%20firmware)
on the `bootloader-version` branch.

## Building

1. Install [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) and the PlatformIO extension.
2. Clone the repository and check out `bootloader-version`.
3. Open the `STEPFOC firmware` folder in VS Code; PlatformIO fetches the platform (`ststm32@15.4.1`) and builds
   with the PlatformIO *Build* button or `pio run`. The image is `.pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin`.

The project is linked for the bootloader: `VECT_TAB_OFFSET=0x3000`, the linker script `ldscript_bootloader.ld`,
the upload offset `0x08003000` and a maximum size of 118784 bytes, in `platformio.ini`. A build that exceeds the
size fails to link.

!!! success "Check"
    PlatformIO ends the build with `SUCCESS`, and `.pio/build/genericSTM32F103CB/firmware.bin` is there. If it
    fails, the first error above the summary names the cause.

## Uploading

PlatformIO runs on Windows, Linux and macOS alike. On Linux, an upload with the programming adapter also needs
PlatformIO's udev rules (`99-platformio-udev.rules`, in the PlatformIO documentation), and a serial port the
`dialout` group.

- **Through the bootloader**: flash the built `firmware.bin` with `bl_flash.py` or Motor GUI as in
  [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/). This is how a release is installed, and works on any driver with
  the bootloader.
- **With the programming adapter**: *Upload* in PlatformIO uses ST-LINK and writes the image at `0x08003000`. It
  leaves the bootloader alone, but it does not update the image CRC the bootloader keeps; see the warning below.
  The serial monitor (the plug icon) opens the UART at 256000 with `send_on_enter`, so you can type commands to
  the driver from the same window.

!!! warning "After an ST-LINK upload the firmware does not start"
    At every power-up the bootloader checks the firmware against the CRC it stored at the last flash through the
    bootloader. After an upload with the programming adapter that CRC no longer matches, so the bootloader stays in
    bootloader mode, with the LED blinking, instead of starting the new firmware. Flash the same `firmware.bin`
    once more through the bootloader to recover. Once the bootloader is on the board, install every firmware
    through it.

![Build, upload and the serial monitor in PlatformIO's status bar.](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/assets/VSUPLOAD.png){ width="700" }

## Where things are

| | |
|---|---|
| `src/constants.h` | `FIRMWARE_VERSION`, the CAN command IDs, the EEPROM map, the loop and PWM frequencies |
| `src/common.h` | the controller and PID structures with their defaults |
| `src/communication.cpp` | the UART command handlers |
| `src/communication_CAN.cpp` | the CAN receive switch and the transmit functions |
| `src/SerialPacketParser.cpp` | the UART parser: it splits a line into the command and its argument (up to 108 it also kept the list of names it accepted) |
| `src/motor_control.cpp` | the control loops, the calibration routine, the gripper state machine |
| `src/bootloader_config.cpp` | the vector table offset and the reset into the bootloader |
| `release_guide.md` | how a release is cut: version bump, build, tag, GitHub release with `firmware.json` |

## Making a release

`release_guide.md` in the repository is the procedure: bump `FIRMWARE_VERSION`, build, commit the source change
with the rebuilt `Binaries/firmware.bin`, tag `V<number>`, create the GitHub release with the image and
`firmware.json` and the release notes. This site's `tools/sync_firmware.py` reads a release by its tag; the
version box names the release.

## A firmware for a board without a bootloader

The `main` branch builds a firmware linked at `0x08000000` for boards that have no bootloader. It stops at
release 103 and is not maintained; install the bootloader instead,
[Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/ -->

# Troubleshooting

By symptom. The error flags and what clears them are in [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/errors/); the
faults of the firmware that are known and not yet fixed, with what to do until they are, in
[Known issues](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/).

## The motor does not move

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A([The motor does not move]) --> B{Does the driver answer?}
    B -- no --> C[The supply and its polarity, the LED;<br>UART: the baud rate, TX and RX;<br>CAN: the node ID, 1 Mbit/s, the termination]
    B -- yes --> D{Calibrated?}
    D -- no --> E[Enter the motor parameters, then #Cal and #Save]
    D -- yes --> F{An error active? The LED on steadily}
    F -- yes --> G[#Error names it: fix the cause, then #Clear]
    F -- no --> H{A current limit above 0?}
    H -- no --> I[#Ilim to the stepper's rated current, #Save]
    H -- yes --> J[Command a setpoint in a closed-loop mode;<br>#Mode and #Info show the state]
```

## The driver does not answer

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| No LED | the supply, DC+ and DC−, the power cable's orientation. If the cable was the wrong way round the driver is destroyed |
| LED on, nothing on the terminal | 256000 baud; TX to RX and RX to TX; the adapter's port; 3.3 V adapter; the line ending CR+LF |
| LED on, nothing on CAN | the node ID; 1 Mbit/s on the adapter; termination (about 60 Ω across CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered); the CAN cable's orientation |
| `Unknown command` | the name's spelling and case: `#Kpiq`, not `#kpiq`; an argument with a space in it (`#WdFb 2000,0,1000,2`, not `#WdFb 2000, 0, 1000, 2`) |
| `Wrong firmware for this board (product lock)`, the LED on steadily | the other product's firmware was flashed: a Spectral Micro image on a STEPFOC. Flash the STEPFOC firmware; the configuration was not touched ([The product lock](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/diagnostics/#the-product-lock)) |
| the LED keeps blinking and nothing answers after a firmware update | the bootloader has no valid firmware, or its CRC does not match after an upload with the programming adapter: flash again through the bootloader, see [Updating through the bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/update/) |

## Motor GUI

| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| the browser offers no port | a Chromium-based browser (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera); Firefox and Safari have no Web Serial |
| the port is listed but will not open | another program holds it: a terminal, PlatformIO's monitor, the Arduino serial monitor |
| the port opens, nothing appears | the driver's power; TX and RX crossed on a non-Source adapter; the baud rate on a non-Source adapter (256000) |
| *No connection* on CAN | the CANvas adapter's port; the bus termination; the node ID of the driver; 1 Mbit/s |
| the calibration does not start | calibration runs over the serial connection only, not over CAN |
| *Unsaved changes* after a power cycle | the settings were not saved to the driver; Save writes them |
| the firmware update finds no bootloader | power-cycle the driver while the GUI scans, to catch the bootloader's 2 s window. A driver with firmware 103 or older from the `main` branch has no bootloader: [Installing the bootloader on an older board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/bootloader/) |

## Calibration

The messages and their causes are in [Motor parameters and calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/). The ones that
come back most:

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| `Magnet test: Failed` | magnet too far, axially magnetised, or missing |
| the motor wobbles left and right during calibration | one coil is not connected |
| the motor does not move in the open-loop step | a coil open or not soldered; calibration then fails at the next step with `Phase order is wrong!` |
| `Phase order is wrong!` | the motor did not respond to the commutation check; wiring, current limit, magnet |
| calibration succeeds, the motor then runs badly or in the wrong direction | the magnet slipped on the shaft; glue it and calibrate again |
| after `Calibration success!` the motor turns slowly by itself for about a minute | the encoder table and the anti-cogging that follow a `#Cal`; let them finish, they save everything ([What follows the calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/#what-follows-the-calibration)) |
| the runs after the calibration stopped: `#Info` shows the encoder table or the anti-cogging not on | a command came in, the shaft was blocked or an error came up; the state is in parameters 52 and 43 ([When a run fails](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/anti-cogging/#checking-them)). `#Save` keeps the calibration; `#Encal all` runs both again |
| the anti-cogging does not switch on (parameter 37 stays 0) | no set is identified for that form; run `#Cogcal save`, or calibrate. After an encoder table measured on its own the set is switched off until it is identified again |
| calibration succeeds but the LED stays on and `#Error` shows nothing | should not happen with firmware 106 and newer, which replaces a damaged configuration block with the defaults at power-up; if `#Info` shows `-1`: `#Default`, parameters, calibrate again |

## The motor

| Symptom | Cause |
|---|---|
| crunching or whining at speed | the current limit or the current loop gains too high; lower `#Ilim`, lower `#Cbw` and calibrate again, or lower `#Kpiq` |
| humming, oscillating at rest | `#Kpv` or `#Kpp` too high; see [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/tuning/) |
| weak torque | `#Ilim` low; the supply's current limit; the wrong `#R`/`#L` (the computed current gains are off) |
| the motor is hot | normal for a stepper at its rated current; lower `#Ilim`, enable the thermistor |
| it stops with a Vbus error when decelerating | the supply cannot absorb the returned energy; a different supply, or a brake resistor |
| it stops with a velocity error | the speed passed 30,000,000 ticks/s, a fixed threshold that `#Vlimit` does not change: a runaway, so check the magnet and the calibration |
| it loses position with a load | that is a torque limit: a stepper under FOC does not lose steps, it falls behind; raise `#Ilim` within the motor's rating, or more motor |
| it holds position with a sawtooth noise | the position loop gain; the magnet distance |

## Low-quality motors

Motors with visibly bad windings, an uneven back-EMF or a resistance that differs between the two coils calibrate
poorly and run rough. The [tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/03-technical-data/tested-motors/) are known good.

## The magnet and the encoder

- The distance is 1 mm. "Magnet Good" from the magnet test does not mean the distance is right, only that the
  field is strong enough.
- A magnet touching the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet too far gives a noisy, wrong position.
- The magnet must be diametrically magnetised and centred on the shaft.

## The driver gets hot or shuts down

The firmware does not monitor the driver stage: if the stage stops on its own, for heat or a short, the motor
loses torque and no error is reported. Lower the current limit, give the board airflow, check the motor leads for
a short. Near 2.8 A the driver needs cooling.

## After a firmware update

`#Info` shows the new release. If the values look wrong or the LED stays on: `#Default`, enter the motor
parameters, `#Cal`, `#Save`. A release note says when an update clears the calibration. After an update to 109,
[Upgrading from older firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/07-firmware/upgrading/) says what to run: a calibration, then the velocity
gains.

A Vbus error right after power-up, cleared by `#Clear`, was the supply ramping up; from firmware 109 a low supply is
not checked in the first 500 ms.

## Getting help

[Support](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/support/) says where to ask and what to include; `#Info`'s output is the first thing.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/known-issues/ -->

# Known issues

The faults in the STEPFOC firmware that are known and not yet fixed, and what to do until they are. The pages that
describe each part say the same where it matters; this page collects them in one place. Which releases work
together is in [Versions and compatibility](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/appendix/compatibility/).

### STEPFOC firmware

Seen in: 109.

| | What happens | What to do | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-3 | The serial number is not read back from the EEPROM at power-up, so `#SERNUM`, Motor GUI and Send_Respond_Device_Info report 1, and every `#Save` writes that 1 over the stored number. | Tell drivers apart by their CAN node ID. To keep a serial number stored, set it with `#SERNUM` before every `#Save`. | [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/saving/) |
| KI-4 | For anyone reading or changing the source, the start values in `common.h` are not the factory defaults (the gripper and calibrated flags start at 1, the pole pairs at 50, `Max_Vbus` at 29500 mV). The EEPROM replaces them at power-up, so a running driver does not show them. | Take the defaults from the Defaults page, which lists what `#Default` writes, or from `Set_Default_config()` in `EEPROM.cpp`. | [Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/defaults/) |
| KI-5 | While the E-stop bit of the last Send_gripper_data_pack (or `#Gripstop 1`) is 1, the driver raises the gripper E-stop error again on every control cycle, so Send_Clear_Error or `#Clear` alone does not clear it. | Send a gripper frame with the E-stop bit 0 (or `#Gripstop 0`) first, then clear the error. | [Gripper mode: moving](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/gripper-mode/#moving) |
| KI-6 | The answer to a 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack goes out before the driver has acted on the command, so its object detection and error bits are those of the moment before, for example 3 (position reached) from the previous move. | Judge the new move by the answers to later frames, or poll with an empty Send_gripper_data_pack. | [Gripper mode: moving](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/gripper-mode/#moving) |
| KI-7 | A 5-byte Send_gripper_data_pack, Send_Clear_Error or `#Clear` during the gripper calibration stops it without a message and leaves its counters as they were, so the next calibration starts part way through; it may skip the opening or give up early. | Send only empty status polls while the gripper calibrates (up to about 24 s). After an interrupted calibration, switch the driver off and on before you calibrate again. | [Gripper mode: calibrating](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/gripper-mode/#calibrating-the-gripper) |
| KI-8 | The action bit in Respond_Gripper_data_pack is a copy of the last command's action bit; the driver never clears it, so it stays 1 after the move has ended. | Tell the end of a move by the object detection, 3 position reached, 1 or 2 stopped on an object. | [Respond_Gripper_data_pack](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/gripper/#respond_gripper_data_pack) |
| KI-9 | Open loop (`#Openloop`, `#gosteps`) puts `#Openv` on the coils without a current limit; `#Ilim` does not apply. The default 5000 mV drives about 4.5 A through a 1.1 Ω coil. | Set `#Openv` to the motor's rated current times its phase resistance first, and keep open-loop tests short. | [Open-loop stepping](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/modes/#open-loop-stepping) |
| KI-10 | The velocity error trips only above a fixed 30,000,000 ticks/s, about 1830 revolutions per second and far above any speed a stepper reaches; `#Vlimit` does not change it, so it does not catch a motor that runs away. | Watch the speed in your host and send Send_Idle or Send_ESTOP when it is wrong. | [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/errors/) |
| KI-11 | Only motion frames and answered status requests reset the watchdog. Setting frames (gains, limits, Idle, Clear) and UART commands do not, so a host that only configures the driver, or a terminal session with a saved watchdog, ends in a watchdog error. | While the watchdog runs, send a status request such as Send_Respond_Encoder_data within every watchdog period. Before you work over UART alone, set the watchdog to 0 over CAN and save. | [Over CAN: a control loop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/can/#a-control-loop) |
| KI-12 | The driver error flag (`Driver_error`, `Driver error` in `#Error`) is never raised. STEPFOC reads no fault output of its driver stage, so a stage that shuts down for heat or a short only makes the motor lose torque, with no error. | Watch the current and the position in your host; a commanded motor that goes limp points to the driver stage. Lower the current limit and give the board air. | [Troubleshooting: the driver gets hot](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/#the-driver-gets-hot-or-shuts-down) |
| KI-13 | `#Dir` stores a flag that `#Info` prints as `Phase direction`, but the control code does not use it: it does not reverse the motor. | To make the other direction positive, negate the setpoints and the values you read back in your host. | [Wiring: phase order and direction](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/04-mounting/wiring/#phase-order-and-direction) |
| KI-14 | `#Mode` prints `Gripper mode` in voltage-torque mode (`#Uq`), and nothing at all in gripper mode, HALL mode, the angle-offset search, open-loop steps (`#gosteps`) and the encoder-table run. | In those modes go by the command you sent last, not by `#Mode`. | [UART commands: status and utility](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/uart/utility/) |
| KI-15 | In idle the driver brakes, with the coils shorted, at every power-up and also with an error; `#Coast` is not kept by `#Save`. The current a turned motor drives through the shorted coils is not limited. | Send `#Coast` (or Send_Settings) after every power-up if the motor must turn freely in idle, and do not let a load drive a braking motor fast. | [Braking in idle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/06-operation/modes/#braking-in-idle) |
| KI-19 | The encoder-table run that follows every `#Cal` holds a field current of 80 % of the current limit for about 20 s. After `#Default` the limit is 1700 mA, so the coils then carry about 1.4 A, more than a smaller stepper is rated for. | Set `#Ilim` for the motor before `#Cal` (a Motor GUI preset sets it). Calibration uses its own limit for its steps and puts yours back before the encoder table runs. | [Calibration: what follows it](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/#what-follows-the-calibration) |

### Fixed

| | What happened | Fixed in | More |
|---|---|---|---|
| KI-1 | The current limit of Send_Limits over CAN is used as sent, also above the driver's 2800 mA; only `#Ilim` over UART clamps it. | 109: Send_Limits stops the current limit at 2800 mA and ignores a negative value | [Send_Limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/reference/can/gains-and-limits/#send_limits) |
| KI-2 | Calibration sets the current limit to 1600 mA and leaves it there, whatever it was before; a `#Save` right after calibration stores the 1600 mA. | 109: calibration puts back the current limit that was in force when it started | [Calibration: save](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/05-setup/calibration/#4-save) |

## Something that is not here

Check the [symptom tables](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/08-troubleshooting/) first. If it is still not explained, [Report a problem](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/109/support/report-a-problem/)
says what to include so it can be reproduced. A fixed issue stays on this page, under "Fixed", with the release
that fixes it.
